transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Dr. Lee. I'm... I'm here, I guess, because my daughter insisted, really, and because people just keep acting like I'm, I don't know, making things up or imagining it all in my head. But I know what I see, and I know what's happening. It started a few weeks ago, maybe a month, when I noticed this white car parked down the street from our house, just sitting there for hours. And then, when I go to work—I clean houses, you know, for an agency—I've seen the same kind of car parked near two of my regular clients' houses. It's not a coincidence. I know the hospital people, the ones who treated my husband last year, and some folks from my cleaning agency, they're... they're working together. They've been watching our house, watching me leave in the morning, following my cleaning routes. I think they're trying to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband, like they don't trust me or something. He had a stroke, you see, and it's been hard, but I do everything for him. I cook, I clean, I manage his pills, but they just won't leave me alone. Every time I look out the front window, I feel like someone is taking notes on me. I tried to tell my supervisor at the agency, but she just looked at me like I was crazy and told me to take some time off. But how can I take time off when they're watching my every move? I just want them to stop.
Besides feeling watched, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you don't seem to notice?

Well... you know, it’s funny you bring that up, because my daughter—she swears up and down that our house is completely silent. But she doesn't live there, does she? She only comes by on Sundays for a couple of hours. During the week, though... especially in the late afternoons when my husband is resting. He has to sleep a lot since the stroke, usually right after I get him settled in his recliner and finish up my cleaning for the day. So the house gets very, very quiet. Just the hum of the old refrigerator, you know how those older models are. 

And... well, even when the house is quiet like that, that's when I hear her. It's a woman's voice. And it's not some muffled sound from the television or the street, it is... it's as clear as if she is standing right there in the room with me, plain as day. She always seems to be right near the kitchen window, the little one above the sink where I do the washing up. And she speaks to me, telling me things I need to do to keep things safe. She'll tell me to go check the locks on the doors, or she'll say I need to move his pills. Just out of nowhere, she'll tell me to move his pills, like they aren't safe where I left them on the counter. 

I always wipe my hands on my apron and look out the glass, thinking maybe it's a neighbor or... or one of those people from the hospital sneaking around the side yard trying to catch me doing something wrong, but there's never anybody out there. But her voice is just so clear, right there by the window, telling me about the locks and the medication. I just don't understand how my daughter can say nothing is happening when I can hear this woman giving me instructions as clearly as I can hear you right now.
Can you tell me exactly how many weeks or months you've been experiencing both the feeling of being watched and hearing this woman's voice, without any break?

Well, let me think back, because time just sort of blurs together when you're dealing with all of this day in and day out, you know? It’s not like you mark it on a calendar. But... if I really sit down and trace it back, past the stroke, past the hospital stays, past all the times I had to rearrange my cleaning schedule just to make sure I was home... it’s been about 11 months. Yes, 11 months now. I remember because it was right around the time the weather started turning last year, when I first started noticing the white car and feeling that prickle on the back of my neck, like eyes were just boring into me. And the voice, the woman by the sink—she started right around then too. Eleven whole months of looking over my shoulder, of checking the locks just like she tells me to, of wondering when those hospital people are finally going to just come up to the door and say whatever it is they want to say. It hasn't stopped, not for a single day, not for a weekend. Just a constant, steady thing for 11 months straight, and it's exhausting, it really is, having to be on guard and listening to her instructions for almost a whole year now without a single break.
During these past 11 months, have you also noticed significant changes in your mood—like feeling very depressed or unusually elated/energetic—that lasted for days or weeks at a time?

Well, it's interesting you ask about my mood, because... yes, I suppose I have noticed something like that. Not depressed, really—Lord knows I don't have the time to sit around feeling sorry for myself with everything I have to manage. But... well, there are these stretches. Sometimes, for a week or maybe two at a time, I wake up and I just feel... bright. That's the only word for it. Just incredibly bright and strong. 

During those times, I feel like I can handle absolutely everything the world throws at me, and then some. I'll get up way before the sun, make my husband's breakfast from scratch, prep all his medications, do a deep clean of my own kitchen—scrubbing the grout, even—and then go out and clean three clients' houses top to bottom without even needing to sit down for a glass of water. I just get this buzzing energy, like I'm running on a fully charged battery and nothing can possibly slow me down. It feels good, honestly, feeling that capable when there's so much pressure on me.

But... the problem is, during those exact same stretches, my patience just completely vanishes. If someone gets in my way or questions me, I just lose my temper so fast. If my husband asks why I moved his recliner two inches to the left, or if one of my clients—like Mrs. Higgins, who is always so terribly particular about her baseboards—if she even hints that I missed a spot or questions how I'm doing my job, I snap. And I mean, I snap much, much harder than I mean to. The words just fly out of my mouth before I can catch them. I'll raise my voice, tell them they don't know what they're talking about, that I have a system and they're ruining it. 

I never used to be quite so sharp-tongued. I've always tried to be patient, especially with my husband since his stroke. But when I get into one of those bright, energetic spells, it's like my fuse is just a quarter-inch long. I feel so on top of everything, so perfectly in control of all the chores and the schedules, that when they question me, it feels like a slap in the face. So I just bite their heads off. It lasts for days, sometimes weeks, where I'm just flying through my work but snapping at anyone who dares to interrupt my flow.
Outside of those bright, energetic stretches you described, during the times when your mood feels more like your usual self, do you still see the watchers and hear the woman's voice just as much?

Well, yes, that's exactly it. That's the thing that really confuses my daughter, I think, because she'll say to me, "Mom, you're so calm today, why are you still talking about the white car?" And it's true, there are definitely times when that buzzing energy just sort of fades away. Like a few months ago, maybe back in early spring? Or was it late winter? The ground was still a bit hard, I remember that much because I was trying to plant some bulbs and the trowel just wouldn't go in. Anyway, there was a spell, probably lasted a good three or four weeks, where I wasn't rushing around cleaning everything in sight. I was actually sleeping a lot more, taking naps in the afternoon while my husband watched his game shows, which I almost never do. I just felt... normal, I suppose. Just going at my regular pace, not feeling that intense need to scrub every surface or snap at Mrs. Higgins about her baseboards. 

But even then... even when I was taking it easy and feeling like my old self, the things going on around me didn't stop. Not at all. I'd wake up from my nap, feeling perfectly rested and calm, and I'd go to the kitchen to start dinner, and there she'd be. The woman's voice, right by the window above the sink. She'd still tell me to check the locks, still tell me to move the pills. And I'd still look out that window and just know, deep down in my bones, that those hospital people—that agency, or whoever they are—were out there watching the house. I'd still see that white car parked halfway down the block. So, yes, even when my mood is perfectly steady and I'm not flying high or losing my temper, the watchers and the voice... they're still there. They don't take a break just because I'm finally getting some rest.
Have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements during this past year that could be contributing to these experiences?

Well, no, absolutely not. I mean, I hardly have time to even think about anything like that, let alone do it. Alcohol? Oh, heavens no. My father, rest his soul, he liked his bourbon a little too much, and I saw what that did to my mother, so I've never been one to touch the stuff. Maybe a sip of champagne at my niece's wedding three years ago, but that's it. And drugs? Goodness, I wouldn't even know where to find them, and I certainly wouldn't take them. My body is a temple, well, mostly, except for my sweet tooth, but I keep that in check. 

As for medications, it's just my usual blood pressure pill that Dr. Evans put me on... oh, it must be five years ago now. A little white pill, I take it every morning with my tea. And I take a multivitamin, just a standard one from the pharmacy down the street, the one with the nice pharmacist, Gary, who always asks about my husband. I did try a new brand of Vitamin C back in the winter because Mrs. Higgins swore it kept her from getting the sniffles, but it upset my stomach so I threw the bottle right in the trash after two days. 

I don't take anything else, I really don't. I'm very careful because I have to manage all of my husband's pills—he has six different ones since the stroke, you know, the blood thinners and the cholesterol ones and the ones for his stomach because the other ones upset his stomach. It's a whole system I have organized in those little plastic daily containers. I have to be sharp to keep his schedule straight, so I wouldn't take anything that would mess with my head. I need all my wits about me to take care of him and keep the house clean and keep an eye on that white car. So, no, nothing new, nothing strange, just my regular routine. I wouldn't dare risk taking anything else with everything I have to juggle right now.
Over these past 11 months, roughly how much of the time would you say you've been in one of those 'bright, energetic' spells versus feeling at your normal, steady baseline?

Well, let me think about that, because eleven months... goodness, that takes us all the way back to last fall, doesn't it? Right around the time the leaves were turning and I had to rake the entire front yard by myself because my husband, well, with his stroke, he can't manage the rake anymore, bless his heart. And if I really look back over all those months, from the raking right through the winter holidays and into the spring and summer... I'd have to say that for most of this whole change I've been going through, I have been just constantly keyed up. 

It's not just a week here or a week there, if I'm being completely honest with you. I mean, the really intense spells where I'm scrubbing the grout at 4 AM and yelling about baseboards, those peak and valley a bit, but even in between those... even in the stretches when things were not at their absolute worst, I've still been so irritable and just driven to keep moving. 

It's like I have this motor humming right under my ribs, and it just refuses to shut off. I'll try to sit down with a cup of chamomile tea, maybe watch a little bit of Jeopardy with my husband—he loves Jeopardy, never misses an episode, he likes to shout the answers at the screen—and I just can't sit there with him. My leg starts bouncing, and I start thinking about the dust on the ceiling fan, or whether I organized the Tupperware drawer properly, or if I need to re-fold the towels so the creases match perfectly, and before I know it, I'm back up on my feet pacing the hallway. 

So, if you're asking how much of the time... I'd say the vast majority of it. Most of the year, really. I just can't seem to settle down. Even when I had that brief spell where I was taking those afternoon naps, like I told you, the minute I woke up, I was right back to feeling wound tight as a spring. I'm just constantly in motion, constantly feeling like if anyone gets in my way or asks me a silly question, I might just snap at them, even on a regular Tuesday when nothing particularly stressful is happening. It's exhausting, honestly, but I just have this overwhelming drive to keep moving, moving, moving, almost all the time.

I just get this buzzing energy, like I'm running on a fully charged battery and nothing can possibly slow me down. It feels good, honestly, feeling that capable when there's so much pressure on me.

But... the problem is, during those exact same stretches, my patience just completely vanishes. If someone gets in my way or questions me, I just lose my temper so fast. If my husband asks why I moved his recliner two inches to the left, or if one of my clients—like Mrs. Higgins, who is always so terribly particular about her baseboards—if she even hints that I missed a spot or questions how I'm doing my job, I snap. And I mean, I snap much, much harder than I mean to. The words just fly out of my mouth before I can catch them. I'll raise my voice, tell them they don't know what they're talking about, that I have a system and they're ruining it. 

I never used to be quite so sharp-tongued. I've always tried to be patient, especially with my husband since his stroke. But when I get into one of those bright, energetic spells, it's like my fuse is just a quarter-inch long. I feel so on top of everything, so perfectly in control of all the chores and the schedules, that when they question me, it feels like a slap in the face. So I just bite their heads off. It lasts for days, sometimes weeks, where I'm just flying through my work but snapping at anyone who dares to interrupt my flow.

inference.note: Added F25.0 (schizoaffective disorder, manic type) given the report of distinct manic-like periods (elevated energy, decreased need for rest, irritability, grandiosity of capability) occurring within the same 11-month timeframe as continuous psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, third-person commanding auditory hallucinations). Need to clarify proportion of time mood symptoms vs. psychotic symptoms alone dominate to differentiate schizophrenia with mood symptoms from schizoaffective disorder.

doctor.question: Outside of those bright, energetic stretches you described, during the times when your mood feels more like your usual self, do you still see the watchers and hear the woman's voice just as much?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a quieter spell for several weeks when I was sleeping more and not rushing around as much, but I still heard the voice by the kitchen window and believed the agency was watching us.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, that's exactly it. That's the thing that really confuses my daughter, I think, because she'll say to me, "Mom, you're so calm today, why are you still talking about the white car?" And it's true, there are definitely times when that buzzing energy just sort of fades away. Like a few months ago, maybe back in early spring? Or was it late winter? The ground was still a bit hard, I remember that much because I was trying to plant some bulbs and the trowel just wouldn't go in. Anyway, there was a spell, probably lasted a good three or four weeks, where I wasn't rushing around cleaning everything in sight. I was actually sleeping a lot more, taking naps in the afternoon while my husband watched his game shows, which I almost never do. I just felt... normal, I suppose. Just going at my regular pace, not feeling that intense need to scrub every surface or snap at Mrs. Higgins about her baseboards. 

But even then... even when I was taking it easy and feeling like my old self, the things going on around me didn't stop. Not at all. I'd wake up from my nap, feeling perfectly rested and calm, and I'd go to the kitchen to start dinner, and there she'd be. The woman's voice, right by the window above the sink. She'd still tell me to check the locks, still tell me to move the pills. And I'd still look out that window and just know, deep down in my bones, that those hospital people—that agency, or whoever they are—were out there watching the house. I'd still see that white car parked halfway down the block. So, yes, even when my mood is perfectly steady and I'm not flying high or losing my temper, the watchers and the voice... they're still there. They don't take a break just because I'm finally getting some rest.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations) have persisted continuously for 11 months, including during a distinct 3-4 week period of normal/euthymic mood with no manic or depressive features. This indicates the mood episodes are not concurrent with the majority of the active psychotic illness, which argues against schizoaffective disorder (F25.0) and supports schizophrenia (F20.0) as the primary diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Rule out substance-induced or medical causes of the psychotic and mood symptoms
doctor.question: Have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements during this past year that could be contributing to these experiences?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the use of alcohol, recreational drugs, or medications/supplements, but my symptom profile does not contain an item related to substance use or medical exclusions.

patient.answer:
Well, no, absolutely not. I mean, I hardly have time to even think about anything like that, let alone do it. Alcohol? Oh, heavens no. My father, rest his soul, he liked his bourbon a little too much, and I saw what that did to my mother, so I've never been one to touch the stuff. Maybe a sip of champagne at my niece's wedding three years ago, but that's it. And drugs? Goodness, I wouldn't even know where to find them, and I certainly wouldn't take them. My body is a temple, well, mostly, except for my sweet tooth, but I keep that in check. 

As for medications, it's just my usual blood pressure pill that Dr. Evans put me on... oh, it must be five years ago now. A little white pill, I take it every morning with my tea. And I take a multivitamin, just a standard one from the pharmacy down the street, the one with the nice pharmacist, Gary, who always asks about my husband. I did try a new brand of Vitamin C back in the winter because Mrs. Higgins swore it kept her from getting the sniffles, but it upset my stomach so I threw the bottle right in the trash after two days. 

I don't take anything else, I really don't. I'm very careful because I have to manage all of my husband's pills—he has six different ones since the stroke, you know, the blood thinners and the cholesterol ones and the ones for his stomach because the other ones upset his stomach. It's a whole system I have organized in those little plastic daily containers. I have to be sharp to keep his schedule straight, so I wouldn't take anything that would mess with my head. I need all my wits about me to take care of him and keep the house clean and keep an eye on that white car. So, no, nothing new, nothing strange, just my regular routine. I wouldn't dare risk taking anything else with everything I have to juggle right now.

inference.note: Persistent psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations) for 11 months that continue even during euthymic periods support schizophrenia; however, presence of distinct hypomanic-like periods with increased energy, decreased need for rest, and irritability raises consideration of schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, pending clarification of proportion of illness time mood symptoms occupy relative to psychosis.

doctor.question: Over these past 11 months, roughly how much of the time would you say you've been in one of those 'bright, energetic' spells versus feeling at your normal, steady baseline?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: For most of this whole change, I have been keyed up, irritable, and driven to keep moving, even in the stretches when things were not at their worst.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the proportion of time spent in the 'bright, energetic' manic state compared to baseline over the course of the illness, which directly addresses whether the manic episode was present for the majority of the total duration.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about that, because eleven months... goodness, that takes us all the way back to last fall, doesn't it? Right around the time the leaves were turning and I had to rake the entire front yard by myself because my husband, well, with his stroke, he can't manage the rake anymore, bless his heart. And if I really look back over all those months, from the raking right through the winter holidays and into the spring and summer... I'd have to say that for most of this whole change I've been going through, I have been just constantly keyed up. 

It's not just a week here or a week there, if I'm being completely honest with you. I mean, the really intense spells where I'm scrubbing the grout at 4 AM and yelling about baseboards, those peak and valley a bit, but even in between those... even in the stretches when things were not at their absolute worst, I've still been so irritable and just driven to keep moving. 

It's like I have this motor humming right under my ribs, and it just refuses to shut off. I'll try to sit down with a cup of chamomile tea, maybe watch a little bit of Jeopardy with my husband—he loves Jeopardy, never misses an episode, he likes to shout the answers at the screen—and I just can't sit there with him. My leg starts bouncing, and I start thinking about the dust on the ceiling fan, or whether I organized the Tupperware drawer properly, or if I need to re-fold the towels so the creases match perfectly, and before I know it, I'm back up on my feet pacing the hallway. 

So, if you're asking how much of the time... I'd say the vast majority of it. Most of the year, really. I just can't seem to settle down. Even when I had that brief spell where I was taking those afternoon naps, like I told you, the minute I woke up, I was right back to feeling wound tight as a spring. I'm just constantly in motion, constantly feeling like if anyone gets in my way or asks me a silly question, I might just snap at them, even on a regular Tuesday when nothing particularly stressful is happening. It's exhausting, honestly, but I just have this overwhelming drive to keep moving, moving, moving, almost all the time.

inference.note: Patient reports psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations) persisting continuously for 11 months, with mood episodes (manic-like periods) present most but not all of that time, and psychotic symptoms clearly present even during euthymic periods (3-4 week stretch without mood symptoms). This pattern of mood symptoms present for majority but not the entirety of the psychotic illness duration, with psychosis persisting independent of mood episodes, fits schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0) rather than schizophrenia (F20.0), which would require mood episodes to be brief relative to total psychotic duration.
